correctness.rationale: For an unchosen edge the two selected endpoint degrees sum to one. Thus any vertex with selected degree at least two has degree d in F. If a chosen edge joins two degree-one vertices, close it and another incident edge into a coordinate square; the two nonendpoints must have selected degree zero, yet their connecting edge would then be undominated. If two degree-d vertices are adjacent, a degree-one neighbor of either one gives a square whose fourth vertex would simultaneously have selected degree zero and be adjacent to a degree-d vertex. Hence the degree-d adjacency forces all neighbors to have degree d, and this propagates by connectivity to the full edge set. Otherwise there is a degree-d vertex (the empty set cannot dominate and degree-one pairs cannot form chosen edges). The degree-one vertices are independent, and the vertices of degrees zero and d together are independent. Connectivity identifies the two classes with the two parities. Each vertex in the degree-one class has exactly one selected neighbor of degree d, giving d|B|=2^(d−1) and |F|=2^(d−1). Thus d is a power of two. Conversely a single-parity center set with exact opposite cover gives precisely one selected incident edge at the opposite endpoint of each unchosen edge and none at its same-parity endpoint. The center set is recoverable as the degree-d vertices, because d≥2, and it is nonempty, so the parity choice is recoverable too. Existence follows by labeling coordinates with the elements of F₂^r: for every odd vertex its syndrome specifies exactly one bit flip to the even zero-syndrome code. This construction is nontrivial since |F| is strictly below the full-edge cardinality. In d=2 these are the four two-edge stars; d=1 is excluded. The supplied check was inspected, not executed; its Q4 loop tests parity-center candidates, not all edge sets.

equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Deleting the last bit identifies each parity class of Q_d with Q_(d−1). The neighbors across the parities map to the same shorter string and all its single flips. Thus the center condition is exactly a classical binary radius-one perfect code, giving the existence construction and its divisibility once the reduction is proved. The old code fact does not make an arbitrary PEDS a same-parity star cover. For d≥2 a full d-star has adjacent chosen edges, so the induced-matching/efficient-edge-domination theorem would not be an equivalent statement.

originality.rationale: The supported distinct claim is the square-forced classification of every non-full PEDS of the Boolean cube, yielding the exact power-of-two obstruction and minimum. It is not the general selected-degree coloring, the construction of Hamming codes, or the use of same-parity induced stars. Closest indexed PEDS results concern other graph families; the same-day Hamming-star lower bound concerns weaker open packing, not a rigidity/converse theorem for all cube PEDSs. Bounded comparison supports this distinction, not absolute priority.

value.rationale: Perfect edge domination is a natural graph invariant distinct from perfect vertex coding or efficient edge domination. The rigidity unifies its existence, exact minimum, and all non-full configurations for an infinite graph family, and reduces any remaining configuration or enumeration problem to a familiar class of perfect codes. The parity rigidity and the uniqueness of the full set in every inadmissible dimension are useful even though the existence construction is classical.
